hint1: My tongue can be almost 50 cm long.
hint2: I have a one-of-a-kind spot pattern.
hint3: I’m the tallest land animal on Earth.
funFacts: A giraffe’s heart can weigh more than 10 kilograms, and it pumps blood all the way up its long neck.

hint1: I spend most of my day curled up asleep in a tree.
hint2: My diet is almost entirely bamboo, even though I'm not closely related to the black-and-white panda.
hint3: I have a bushy ringed tail and a reddish coat, and people sometimes call me a 'red cat-bear.'
funFacts: Red pandas use their bushy tails as blankets in cold weather and have a false thumb, an extended wrist bone, that helps them grip bamboo stems.
imageAttribution: Photo: Bernard Landgraf, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

hint1: I live so deep underwater that the pressure would crush most other fish.
hint2: Out of the water, gravity makes me look nothing like I do in my natural habitat.
hint3: I've been voted one of the world's ugliest animals, and my saggy face is famous online.
funFacts: A blobfish's body is mostly a gel-like substance slightly less dense than water, letting it float just above the sea floor without wasting energy swimming.
imageAttribution: Photo: Alphama, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

hint1: I'm the only mammal in the world completely covered in scales.
hint2: When I feel threatened, I roll up into a tight, armored ball.
hint3: I use a long, sticky tongue to slurp up ants and termites, much like an anteater.
funFacts: A pangolin's tongue can be longer than its own body, and it retracts into a pouch near its pelvis when not in use.
imageAttribution: Photo: Ari hidayat99, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

hint1: I live year-round in cold Arctic waters.
hint2: Males of my species usually grow a single long, spiraled tusk.
hint3: That tusk is actually an overgrown tooth, and it's inspired centuries of unicorn legends.
funFacts: A narwhal's tusk is a canine tooth that can grow up to 3 meters long and is packed with nerve endings, possibly helping it sense changes in the water.
imageAttribution: Photo: The Public Domain Review, Public Domain, Wikimedia Commons

hint1: I lay eggs, even though I'm a mammal.
hint2: I have a soft, sensitive bill that I use to detect prey underwater.
hint3: I look like a mix of a duck, a beaver, and an otter, and the males among us have a venomous spur on their hind legs.
funFacts: When platypuses were first described to European scientists, many believed the pelt was an elaborate hoax stitched together from other animals.
imageAttribution: Photo: TwoWings, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

hint1: I never really grow up, I keep my juvenile features my whole life.
hint2: If I lose a limb, or even part of my heart or brain, I can regrow it.
hint3: I'm a salamander with feathery external gills and a face that always looks like it's smiling.
funFacts: Axolotls are critically endangered in the wild in Mexico, even though they're one of the most common amphibians kept in captivity worldwide.
imageAttribution: Photo: Marius Maehlen (Mariblubb), CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

hint1: Each of my eyes can swivel and focus independently of the other.
hint2: I'm famous for changing color, though it's more about mood and temperature than blending in.
hint3: I have a long, sticky tongue I can shoot out faster than a blink to catch insects.
funFacts: A chameleon's tongue can extend to more than one and a half times its own body length and accelerates faster than a fighter jet.
imageAttribution: Photo: Zeynel Cebeci, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

hint1: I move so slowly that algae grows in my fur.
hint2: I spend almost my entire life hanging upside down in trees.
hint3: I'm famous as one of the slowest-moving mammals on Earth.
funFacts: Sloths only leave their trees to go to the bathroom about once a week, and the trip can be dangerous since it's when they're most vulnerable to predators.
imageAttribution: Photo: Krunal Desai, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

hint1: In my species, it's the males who carry the babies, not the females.
hint2: I swim upright, and I'm a famously weak swimmer despite living in the open ocean.
hint3: My head looks like a horse's, which is exactly how I got my name.
funFacts: Male seahorses carry fertilized eggs in a specialized pouch and give birth to fully-formed babies, one of the only examples of male pregnancy in the animal kingdom.
imageAttribution: Photo: FASTILY, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

hint1: I have three hearts and blue blood.
hint2: I can squeeze my entire boneless body through any gap bigger than my beak.
hint3: I have eight arms lined with suckers, and I'm famous for being one of the smartest invertebrates alive.
funFacts: An octopus can change both the color and texture of its skin in less than a second to blend almost perfectly into its surroundings.
imageAttribution: Photo: Martijn Klijnstra, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

hint1: The pink or reddish color of my feathers actually comes from what I eat.
hint2: I usually stand and sleep balanced on just one leg.
hint3: I'm known for my long legs, curved neck, and bright pink feathers, and I usually live in large flocks.
funFacts: Flamingos get their pink color from pigments in the algae and shrimp they eat, and in captivity they can turn pale without the right diet.
imageAttribution: Photo: Charles J. Sharp, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

hint1: I make one of the longest migrations of any insect on Earth.
hint2: My caterpillar stage eats almost nothing but milkweed, which makes me toxic to most predators.
hint3: I'm an orange-and-black butterfly, and no single one of us completes the whole migration round trip, it takes multiple generations.
funFacts: Monarch butterflies that migrate south in the fall can live up to 8 months, far longer than the few weeks a typical summer generation survives.
imageAttribution: Photo: Charles Patrick Ewing, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

hint1: I sleep around 20 hours a day.
hint2: My diet is almost entirely eucalyptus leaves, which are toxic to most other animals.
hint3: I'm a tree-dwelling marsupial from Australia, often mistaken for a bear, even though I'm not one.
funFacts: Koalas have fingerprints so similar to human fingerprints that they can be difficult to tell apart even under a microscope.
imageAttribution: Photo: Diliff (David Iliff), CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons
